title: The Reservation Inflation of Hard Money: Gold-Standard Deflation and the Real Expansion of Nominal Claims, 1873-1896
summary: This academic paper tests the SCR (Scarcity-Credence-Reserve) monetary theory by examining the 1873-1896 gold-standard deflation period, finding that while circulation inflation (measured by CPI) turned negative in both Britain and the US, reservation inflation (measured by real value of fixed nominal claims) turned positive. The paper argues this demonstrates that hard money does not eliminate inflationary pressure but merely shifts its domain of expression from transaction prices to the real burden of nominal debt.
key_points: The SCR theory proposes two distinct expressions of inflation: circulation inflation (rising transaction prices) and reservation inflation (rising real weight of monetary symbols and debt contracts)
Between 1873-1896, Britain's price index fell from 18.0 to 14.7, while US historical CPI fell from 36.0 to 25.0, representing classic gold-standard deflation
Despite negative circulation inflation, fixed-claim reservation index rose 22.4% in Britain and 44.0% in the US, indicating mechanically increased real value of nominal claims
The paper supports a phase-dependent view of inflation where CPI is only one observable expression of monetary-material asymmetry
Authored by Ran Huang, categorized under econ.GN (economics general) on arXiv
why_it_matters: This paper provides a theoretical framework for understanding how monetary regimes affect inflation expression. While purely academic, it challenges conventional wisdom that deflationary monetary regimes eliminate inflationary pressures—instead suggesting these pressures manifest in different forms (reservation vs. circulation inflation). For macro analysis, it suggests that CPI alone may understate inflationary pressure under certain monetary conditions.
macro_context: The paper offers a theoretical lens for understanding historical monetary dynamics during the classical gold standard. It is not a current macro catalyst but rather a historical academic study proposing a phase-dependent view of inflation where CPI captures only one expression of monetary-material asymmetry. The Japan companion paper showed monetary-base expansion no longer translated strongly into consumer-price inflation after entering a 'reserve-dominant phase'.
